title: Family of man shot by Hamilton police want 'truth and transparency,' a call echoed by politicians
subtitle: Erixon Kabera was a family man, "had no issues" with police, say relatives and friends.
article: Andy Ganza didn't think much when he arrived at his best friend's west Hamilton condo building Saturday night to find police blocking the entrance.
"I just thought it was an accident," he said.
His suspicion of something more serious grew as he took a detour around the building at 1964 Main St. W. and spotted more officers, blocked entrances and yellow tape.

Eventually, Ganza parked his car on Wilson Street East and headed for the building on foot. He said he phoned his buddy 10 to 15 times on the way. None of his calls were answered. Not hearing from his friend wasn't unusual - the pair hung out almost daily, often dropping in without setting a time. They were bonded by their Rwandan heritage and passion for faith, family and community.
"Either he's sleeping, he's in the shower or whatever; he lives by himself so maybe he was just on the couch or something," Ganza remembered thinking.

"I even took a small video (of the police presence) and I texted him, 'Wake up so you can tell me ... do you see what's going on in your building?' Nothing about, 'Are you OK yourself?' because that never entered my mind."
It was unimaginable to Ganza that the large police presence had anything to do with his friend, so he left. Later that night, he got the call that his friend was shot by police.
Erixon Kabera, known since he was a kid by his nickname Gentil, was pronounced dead at 2:47 a.m. Sunday.
In the days since, Kabera's family and friends have been searching for answers. Local politicians also echoed that call on Tuesday.
"We want to know exactly what happened and quickly," Yves Ikobe, one of Kabera's brothers said.
"I really want the truth and transparency."

The search for answers has been more complicated because of inaccurate information in the immediate aftermath of the shooting when the Special Investigations Unit - an arm's length agency that investigates police shootings - said the shooting happened in an exchange of gunfire. Kabera's loved ones were baffled because the man they knew was peaceful, a dedicated father and community builder.

The SIU later clarified that two officers shot at the 43-year-old in the 5th-floor hallway of the building after an "interaction." Investigators later found a replica firearm in the hallway, the SIU said Wednesday, but have not explained how it may have been used in the interaction.

Hamilton police say they were called to the building after a resident reported a man outside her door she believed had a gun. Police can only comment on what led up to the incident, not the shooting itself, because of the ongoing SIU investigation.
It's not clear what happened after police responded, but the SIU says two officers fired their guns in the hallway and two other officers have been designated witnesses.

Kabera's family and friends say nothing about what they've heard makes sense. They never knew him to have guns, including replica firearms. He also never complained about having issues with neighbours, nor were they aware of any serious mental health issues.

Kabera is the father of three boys ranging in age from 10 to 17 who often stay with their dad at the apartment where he has lived the last couple of years. They were not staying with him Saturday and family believe he was alone, packing for a planned moved to Montreal the next day where he was looking to work with his uncle on a food distribution business while also travelling back to Hamilton to see his children.

Kabera came to Canada from Rwanda in 2005 and lived with his wife and then children in Toronto for many years, before coming to Hamilton several years ago for a "better life" for his boys," Ikobe said.

Both in Toronto and in Hamilton, his brother was involved in the Rwandan community, organizing events, helping newcomers with documentation and volunteering. In Hamilton, this volunteer work included a relationship with Hamilton police, organizing annual events where the two groups got together to play sports.
"He had no issues with police," Ikobe said.
Proficient in both French and English, he worked taking reported fraud calls for a bank, and later for seven years as a resource officer for Canada Revenue Agency.
"He was a very kind guy," his brother said.

There were five siblings in the family, with two brothers following Kabera to Canada and two other siblings staying behind. If there was a family event, such as a wedding, he always found a way to travel home to celebrate.
When Ikobe last spoke to his brother the day before the shooting, Kabera was in a "pretty good mood." Ganza similarly described his friend as sounding "normal" in their phone call earlier Saturday.
As they wait for answers, so do local politicians, who in a statement Tuesday called for greater transparency in the investigation.

"There are so many unanswered questions that must be addressed in a full, timely and transparent manner," Hamilton Centre MP Matthew Green, MPP Sara Jama and anti-racism activist Kojo Damptey said in the statement.
The statement said reports of suspicious activity in the area prior to the shooting "appear to be questionable and racially loaded." It also took issue with communication around the shooting.
On Wednesday, Chief Frank Bergen released his own statement in a bid to clear up "factual inaccuracies."
"I know there are many unanswered questions and I trust the SIU will work to address these in a full, timely, transparent manner," added Bergen, who expressed condolences to the victim's family.
"I have been in touch with Rwandan community leaders and made ourselves available to meet when the community is ready."
Also on Wednesday, the Hamilton Police Association hit out at "ignorant commentary" they said casts "judgement upon our officers" and "inflames an already tragic situation."
"(The SIU's) report will shed light on the totality of the interaction in due course," the association said in a statement.

Kabera's family is holding a vigil outside city hall at 6 p.m. Thursday to commemorate the father of three's life and demand answers about why it was cut short. A GoFundMe has been created to cover funeral and potential legal costs.
